item.title: Tech Stocks Tumble on Worries Over A.I. Spending and China’s Chips
item.description:
A global technology stock sell-off intensified on Tuesday, underpinned by worries over hefty bills for the build-out of artificial intelligence systems and concerns over tougher competition from China.

The Nasdaq Composite index, chock-full of big technology companies, came close on Tuesday to falling into correction, Wall Street’s term of a drop of 10 percent or more from its recent peak, before rebounding to trade flat for the day. The American chip company Micron fell over 7 percent in early trading on Tuesday, as did Advanced Micro Devices. Nvidia, the leading chipmaker, nudged lower before turning higher, but it remains more than 15 percent below its peak in May. SpaceX, Elon Musk’s rocket and A.I. company, also rebounded from an early morning slide. The stock remains more than 40 percent below its June peak.

The bumpy sell-off has taken hold over the past month, as fears about the ballooning spending by big technology companies on A.I. infrastructure and the threat of cheaper competitors undermining it have come to the fore. Cheaper A.I. models threaten the dominance of a handful of U.S.-listed companies, while competition from China has loosened South Korea’s grip on the market for memory chips critical to A.I.

On Tuesday, South Korea’s benchmark KOSPI index plunged nearly 11 percent, at one point triggering a temporary trading halt. The index has lost a third of its value over the past month but remains over 40 percent higher for the year because of the soaring rally that preceded the recent drop. Benchmark indexes in Japan and Taiwan both fell around 4 percent. Stocks in China fell over 2 percent.

The drop in South Korea spread to American exchanges. The Nasdaq 100 index, which strips out banks from the broader index making it further dependent on big tech companies, fell over 1 percent in early trading and is heading into afternoon trading almost 10 percent below its peak in June.

In Europe, the German chipmaker Infineon fell nearly 7 percent, and the Dutch semiconductor equipment maker ASML shed 3.5 percent. The Dow Jones industrial average, which is far less exposed to the tech industry, rose 1 percent on Tuesday, a sign that investors are homing in on concerns surrounding A.I.

The latest market tremor began on Monday, when the shares of China’s leading memory chipmaker, ChangXin Memory Technologies, began trading after a blockbuster initial public offering. The company’s stock soared nearly 500 percent on its market debut, quickly making it the most valuable company on the Shanghai exchange. It slipped 4 percent on Tuesday.

The listing prompted widespread fears that intensifying industry competition could threaten rival global memory chipmakers in South Korea, Japan, Taiwan and the United States.

Rising spending forecasts from the tech firms leading the A.I. infrastructure build out are also fanning fears. The recent market jitters intensify the spotlight on the big tech companies reporting financial results this week. Meta, Microsoft and SK Hynix, South Korea’s semiconductor giant, are set to report on Wednesday, and Apple and Amazon on Thursday.

The declines in Asia began as soon as stocks started trading on Tuesday, with A.I. and semiconductor stocks hit the hardest. Japanese flash memory maker Kioxia fell more than 18 percent. South Korean semiconductor company Samsung Electronics dropped about 13 percent.

Asian markets have been trending downward since late June, weighed down by recurring concerns over the sustainability of this year’s A.I. rally.

The staggering scale of spending required to keep up in the global A.I. race was highlighted this week with OpenAI, the parent of ChatGPT, nearing a deal to lease a $500 billion data center in Ohio, supported by $250 billion in financial backing from Nvidia. Last week, earnings reported by Tesla and Alphabet, Google’s parent company, shook the markets as they revealed their own enormous A.I. spending needs.

On Monday, the Chinese start-up Moonshot publicly released the details of its latest A.I. model, adding to investor concerns about China catching up to the United States in the A.I. arms race.

The latest market turmoil is an unwelcome turn for a region where the A.I. boom has served as a rare economic bright spot. In markets like South Korea and Taiwan, rising chip exports and soaring A.I. valuations have masked broader weakness across their domestic economies, which remain heavily dependent on energy imports from the Middle East.

The war in Iran, another major worry for investors, has rattled markets recently by restricting oil exports from the Persian Gulf and Red Sea, pushing up oil and gas prices. President Trump said on Monday that there was “a good chance” that a new round of diplomatic talks could yield a breakthrough in the monthslong war.

A recent pause in fighting has helped ease oil prices, with Brent crude, the international benchmark, falling to around $84 a barrel on Tuesday. Still, the cost of crude is up more than 15 percent since the start of the war, feeding into higher prices for gasoline and a wide range of products derived from petroleum.

item.title: The Chips Rout Goes Global
item.description:
Andrew here. Chipmakers are taking a hit this morning because investors worry that Big Tech’s extravagant artificial intelligence spending isn’t delivering real profits yet. At the same time, powerful open-weight models are making A.I. cheaper to run, raising questions about whether companies need to keep buying such expensive tech, including chips.

Still, there are huge long-term investment build-out commitments from major tech players. So, the big question: Is this just a healthy reset for a hot market, or the start of a bigger slowdown?

Also: Make sure to read Bernard Arnault’s reply to a critical series of articles in Le Monde about LVMH. It is quite a read. More below.

Not long ago, chipmakers central to the artificial intelligence boom were the hottest trade on Wall Street.

Now investors are reckoning with headwinds that could put that sector’s gains at risk. Those concerns are playing out across global markets on the eve of a momentous string of tech earnings reports.

The latest:

South Korea’s Kospi index, home to chip giants SK Hynix and Samsung, plunged more than 10 percent on Tuesday in extremely volatile trading. The loss shaved nearly $600 billion off SK Hynix’s market cap.

S&P 500 futures are under pressure, also being dragged down by tech companies.

Nvidia tumbled 5 percent on Monday. The roughly $250 billion rout saw the chipmaker lose its crown as the world’s most valuable listed company (to Apple).

A trio of factors are driving the sell-off: Investors are concerned about a breakneck A.I. spending spree, circular financing in the sector and growing Chinese competition.

Numbers to watch:

The four biggest hyperscalers — Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft — are forecast to spend a combined $5.3 trillion on capital expenditure through 2030, much of it to finance their A.I. ambitions, according to Goldman Sachs.

This year, hyperscalers are set to borrow up to $400 billion to pay for that infrastructure build-out, according to S&P Global, a market data firm. The scale of borrowing is beginning to unnerve some in the bond market, especially as concerns grow that the Fed may raise interest rates to tamp down wartime inflation.

And then there’s the circular question. Nvidia, AMD and other chipmakers have pledged billions of dollars to A.I. companies. Some analysts wonder if these are legitimate investments or a form of vendor financing to prop up the start-ups that are also their biggest customers.

Those concerns re-emerged on Monday on reports, including from The Wall Street Journal and The Times, that Nvidia is in talks with OpenAI to provide the ChatGPT maker with a $250 billion financial backstop to help cover lease costs on a $500 billion data center in Ohio.

Will tech bosses reassure investors? Chipmakers — SK Hynix and Samsung — and hyperscalers — Meta, Microsoft and Amazon — report quarterly results on Wednesday and Thursday. From the latter trio, investors will want more insight into when their mammoth A.I. bets will pay off.

For chip giants, the big focus will be on demand for their hardware, and how they are positioned to fend off a growing threat from Chinese rivals.

Oil prices fall again. Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, eased to $86.65 this morning as a pause in U.S. fighting with Iran extended into a fourth day. President Trump said on Monday that there was “a good chance” negotiations with Tehran could yield a more lasting peace deal. Iranian officials appear less upbeat.

Johnson & Johnson reaches a deal to settle decade-old talc lawsuits. The company agreed to pay $5.5 billion to settle about 80,000 suits that claim that its talc products caused ovarian cancer. J&J has seen several settlement deals fall through before, but there appears to be more optimism this time.

Minnesota’s ban on prediction markets is in doubt. A federal judge sided with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, and Kalshi and Polymarket, the prediction markets companies, which sued to stop the ban, arguing that the platforms can only be regulated at the federal level. The C.F.T.C. has sued more than a dozen states that have tried to use anti-gambling laws to block prediction market trading.

Shares in LVMH are gaining in Paris this morning on renewed hopes of a turnaround at the luxury-goods conglomerate that’s home to Dior handbags and Hennessy cognac.

But the thing everyone seems to be talking about is Bernard Arnault’s social media savoir-faire.

A recap: On Sunday, the fashion tycoon delivered a rebuttal to Le Monde’s six-part series investigating potential ruptures in the Arnault family power structure.

The 77-year-old wrote an open letter dripping with sarcasm, titled “Merci,” that the company posted on X and was quickly translated into English by users. It was a defense of his business and family replete with the following zingers:

I learned, first of all, that my staff are impeccably turned out and not one of them is overweight. I offer apologies to readers for this failure of bodily diversity, and I shall raise the matter with the company canteen.

And then:

…comes “the business-first strategy.” That a group exporting most of its French-made products should place commerce somewhere in its strategy, it appears, qualifies as a scoop. I await the follow-ups: L’Oréal sells beauty products, Danone takes an interest in food, Renault makes cars, and so on. We can keep this going until Christmas.

And finally:

… the crowning touch: the family. Once cannot write about a man for six months without ending up, in thought, at his table. There I found my five children, my wife, my nephews. I would have liked to find one nuance: the one that lets five strong personalities work in the same house without turning it into Italian opera. At the Arnault family, apparently, we don’t argue, we conspire. We don’t deliberate, we plot. Very novelistic. In the real world, my children run Maisons, build teams, make decisions and — sacrilege — call one another on Sundays.

In what could be viewed as a victory lap of sorts, Arnault made his first post on Monday on X under his personal account. He thanked those who cheered his open letter (and gave his Le Monde critique more oxygen).

The open letter has generated roughly 9 million views, garnering hat tips from X’s former C.E.O. Linda Yaccarino (a “masterclass!,” she raved), the billionaire investor Dan Loeb and Alfred Lin, a partner at Sequoia.

President Trump’s embrace of crypto has been astonishingly profitable, netting him roughly $1.4 billion last year alone.

Much of that windfall came through World Liberty Financial. The company, run by Trump’s sons and the sons of Steve Witkoff, a Trump adviser, has cultivated a lucrative trade in $WLFI digital tokens. Now it has spawned a legal battle, pitting the company against an early investor, the crypto billionaire Justin Sun.

The Chinese-born founder of the crypto exchange Tron became an adviser to the company in 2024 and invested a total of $75 million.

But Sun sued World Liberty in federal court in April, accusing it of fraud, breach of contract and extortion. He claims that World Liberty froze his tokens after he refused to invest more money.

Sun says he believes World Liberty is giving crypto a bad name, and the breakup is getting messy, as Jen Wieczner writes in New York magazine:

Sun would come to believe he’d made a colossal mistake. World Liberty would disappoint his expectations and those of many other investors: The decentralized crypto products it promised would largely never materialize; the money investors put in would remain mostly locked away from them; and the $WLFI cryptocurrency would crash, leaving many token holders with huge losses while the president and his partners made hundreds of millions in profits. Sun would be stripped of his tokens entirely. “Today, the thing I regret the most is not only that my money got stuck but that my name is on the project,” Sun says.

World Liberty countered by suing Sun for defamation in May in Florida state court. The company accuses Sun of betting against its tokens and embarking on a “public smear campaign.”

The billionaire says it’s his duty to call out World Liberty’s bad behavior. But Sun himself has a rocky legal track record, and a less-than-sterling reputation. Wieczner writes:

Many in that industry dismiss the claims as a pot-versus-kettle situation. “It’s scammers scamming scammers,” more than one crypto investor told me.

One year ago today, a gunman walked into an office building in Midtown Manhattan with an assault rifle and killed four people.

Among those who died was Wesley LePatner, a senior executive at the private equity firm Blackstone. On Tuesday, LePatner’s husband, Evan LePatner, is introducing the Wesley Mittman LePatner Foundation in honor of his wife.

The foundation’s goal is to encourage business leaders to take on leadership roles in nonprofit organizations. It is launching in New York and aims to train 1,000 leaders nationwide to carry forward LePatner’s legacy of balancing professional success with philanthropic and civic engagement.

“Wesley was a born leader,” Evan LePatner told Niko Gallogly. The two met during their freshman year of college at Yale. They married in 2006 and had two children together.

LePatner started her career at Goldman Sachs, before joining Blackstone in 2014. She was one of Blackstone’s top-ranking women leaders and became the C.E.O. of Blackstone Real Estate Income Trust in January 2025. She was known for mentoring colleagues, especially other women navigating the male-dominated financial industry.

“I felt so strongly from the moment after she died that I had to keep her flame going,” Evan LePatner said. “She had this pulsating energy.”

She founded the Altneu Synagogue in New York and served as a board member of UJA-Federation of New York, a charitable organization focused on Jewish causes, and the Metropolitan Museum of Art.

The foundation aims to help young professionals follow in her footsteps. Evan LePatner said it will connect them with service-minded mentors. The hope is that it will lead to opportunities for them to serve on boards and partner with nonprofits and civic organizations.

The organization’s advisory board includes Ken Caplan, the global co-chief investment officer of Blackstone; Brian Friedman, the president of the investment bank Jefferies; Chris Lee, a partner at the private equity firm KKR, and others.

Evan LePatner will serve as the chair of the foundation, a position he said he will balance alongside his full-time role as managing partner at the private equity firm he founded, Courizon Partners, and raising his two teenage children.

“Wesley was the expert juggler,” he said. “I have become better than I ever thought I could be, but I’m still junior league compared to her.”

Deals

David Ellison, Paramount’s C.E.O., told staff that he is “highly confident” the merger with Warner Bros Discovery will close, despite recent legal setbacks. (Bloomberg)

Ares Management, the investment group, reportedly has held talks to acquire the private equity firm Leonard Green & Partners. (FT)

Tech and artificial intelligence

“How Meta Got Everything It Wanted in a Secret Louisiana Data Center Deal” (NYT)

Dario Amodei, the C.E.O. of Anthropic, denied that his A.I. company is pushing to ban open-weight models like those made by Chinese rivals — as Beijing warned of retaliation if the U.S. was weighing such a clampdown. (CNBC, Bloomberg)

Best of the rest

“Ex-JPMorgan Banker Chirayu Rana Files New Lawsuit — and It’s Totally Different From His ‘Sex Slave’ Claims” (NY Post)

The F.B.I. seized the cellphone of Mark Walter, the owner of the Los Angeles Dodgers, as part of an investigation into his asset-management firm, Guggenheim Investments, that began with a whistle-blower complaint. (Bloomberg, WSJ)

We’d like your feedback! Please email thoughts and suggestions to dealbook@nytimes.com.

item.title: Boeing Reports Loss on $280 Million Hit to Troubled Air Force One Program
item.description:
Boeing’s troubled Air Force One program incurred another cost overrun in the three months that ended in June, contributing to a bigger-than-expected $428 million loss in the second quarter of 2026.

The company’s effort to build two presidential planes has been hampered by delays and unexpected costs since it agreed to make them in 2018 at a fixed price of $3.9 billion. Boeing said production and certification expenses added $280 million to its costs in the second quarter. The planes were expected to be delivered in 2024, but that date has been pushed to 2028 after frequent cost overruns.

Those delays contributed to President Trump’s decision to retrofit a jet gifted to the United States by the Qatari royal family as a temporary Air Force One replacement. But Mr. Trump’s push to adapt that aircraft has resulted in ballooning costs and safety trade-offs. This month, Mr. Trump flew out of Turkey on the old Air Force One at the urging of the Secret Service.

Despite the quarterly loss, which was more than double what was expected, Boeing’s turnaround efforts are gaining momentum. The company started a fourth production line this month for the 737 Max, its most popular plane by far. The expansion is expected to help Boeing produce more of the planes, which account for a majority of its more than half-trillion-dollar order backlog. And Boeing said a measure of cash flow was positive in the quarter, a sign of progress as the firm digs out from under a large amount of accumulated debt.

The company has also regained the trust of the Federal Aviation Administration, which has loosened some restrictions placed on Boeing after recent crises. Its 737 Max jets were grounded worldwide for nearly two years after design flaws contributed to fatal crashes in 2018 and 2019, in which 346 people died. In 2024, Being faced another crisis when a panel door blew off during a flight, the result of poor production practices. Boeing undertook several leadership and culture changes to address those problems.

This month, the F.A.A. said it would let Boeing resume signing off on its 737 Max and 787 planes after removing those privileges in 2019 and again in 2022. The agency said it had made that decision after “months of thorough data and safety review demonstrating consistent production quality.”

item.title: Gibson Dunn Hires Rival Wachtell Lipton’s Co-Chair
item.description:
In the latest skirmish in the fight for legal talent, the law firm Gibson Dunn said it had hired one of the co-chairs of rival Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, as well as five other partners in its litigation department.

Gibson Dunn’s hiring of William Savitt, who has served as Wachtell’s co-chair since 2023, highlights the fierce competition for top lawyers at a time when deals, the lifeblood of the big law industry, are booming and business becomes more legally complex. That competition is putting pressure on long-held loyalties.

Just this week, the law firms Simpson Thacher, Kirkland & Ellis and Paul Weiss announced a flurry of hires they had made from rival firms, as they look to bulk up in capital markets and restructuring. The Financial Times earlier reported the news of Mr. Savitt’s move.

For decades, Wachtell has stood out on Wall Street for its simple model: a tightknit, single-office boutique in New York with intellectual firepower and expertise in mergers and acquisitions and corporate litigation in Delaware Chancery Court, considered the foremost destination for adjudicating corporate disagreements.

Mr. Savitt, who joined Wachtell in 2000, led many of those more recent litigation battles, including successfully defending Twitter in its lawsuit that forced Elon Musk to close his $44 billion acquisition of the company.

This spring, he served as lead counsel for OpenAI during a high-profile trial in which the company successfully defended itself against Mr. Musk’s accusations of a breach of contract. Mr. Savitt gained attention for his at times combative cross-examination of Mr. Musk on the witness stand.

Wachtell continues its work on other high-profile matters, including representing Jefferies in litigation surrounding the bankruptcy of the auto parts maker First Brands.

“Wachtell Lipton is performing at its highest level across every metric,” a spokeswoman for the firm said in a statement.

The prospect of hiring Mr. Savitt was “a dream hatched” when Barbara Becker became chair of Gibson Dunn five years ago, she said in an interview on Tuesday. Mr. Savitt was “No. 1 on that list,” Ms. Becker said, “never thinking in a million years that it would come to pass.”

Since taking over as chair in 2021, Ms. Becker has made a number of other big hires to broaden the firm’s reach. This year, the firm hired a group of appellate lawyers from Sullivan & Cromwell, including Jeff Wall, a former acting U.S. solicitor general, and in 2024 it brought on a group led by Barry Berke, a prominent white-collar defense lawyer.

Gibson Dunn’s focus on hiring high-powered litigators is also notable because other firms, like Paul Weiss, have seen a fracturing of their corporate and litigation departments.

“You can’t do an M&A deal of any scale without understanding fundamentally the litigation playing field,” said Orin Snyder, co-chair of Gibson Dunn’s trials practice group, who has known Mr. Savitt for years.

Joining Mr. Savitt at Gibson Dunn’s New York office are five other lawyers from Wachtell: Sarah Eddy, Randall Jackson, Ryan McLeod, Anitha Reddy and Brad Wilson.

item.title: Writers Guild Withdraws Support From Film Festival Over A.I.
item.description:
A new flashpoint emerged on Tuesday in the debate over artificial intelligence and artistic expression.

The dispute involves Urbanworld, a New York festival that showcases Black and multicultural films, and the Writers Guild of America East, a 6,000-member union that represents movie, television, podcast and digital news writers. In a letter sent to staff and supporters, Urbanworld’s founder, Stacy Spikes, said the guild had “withdrawn its sponsorship and participation in this year’s festival” over his decision to add films made with A.I. tools.

“We are deeply disappointed,” Spikes wrote in the letter, a copy of which was viewed by The New York Times. “For the past decade, the W.G.A.E. has been one of Urbanworld’s most valued partners.”

A spokesman for the guild did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The union has been among the entertainment industry’s loudest voices on the dangers of generative A.I., using its #AINeedsHumans campaign to push for worker protections and transparency.

An Urbanworld spokesman declined to disclose the financial value of the guild’s withdrawn support. Urbanworld has not revealed its sponsorship list for this year’s festival, which begins Oct. 14. Sponsors in 2025 included HBO, Warner Bros. Discovery, Netflix and the Directors Guild of America, according to the Urbanworld website.

The festival has given a platform to Ryan Coogler, Ava DuVernay, Cord Jefferson and other filmmakers since its founding in 1997. Last month, Spikes announced a new programming section called A.I. Sidebar for directors who use generative A.I. and related digital tools to create their work.

“Rather than ignore those projects or force them into categories that were never designed to evaluate them, we believed the more transparent and responsible approach was to create a dedicated space where they could be viewed, discussed and judged alongside comparable work,” Spikes wrote.

He added: “We understand why artificial intelligence has become one of the most debated issues facing the creative community. Questions surrounding authorship, compensation, consent, employment, creative ownership and the future of creative work deserve serious discussion.”

Festival programmers have generally resisted treating A.I. filmmaking as its own artistic category. Some festivals, including Cannes, have banned from competition films made with heavy reliance on A.I. tools. Others have shown a willingness to explore, including the Tribeca Festival, which recently showcased a film created entirely with A.I. — no actors, no sets, no cameras — as part of its official lineup.

“We believe the answer is engagement, not absence,” Spikes said in his letter.

item.title: Ross Douthat Joins ‘60 Minutes’ as a Correspondent
item.description:
Ross Douthat, an opinion columnist at The New York Times, is leaving to join the CBS News program “60 Minutes” as a correspondent, the show’s executive producer said in a memo to staff on Tuesday.

Mr. Douthat is among a group of journalists joining for the show’s 59th season, which will premiere on Sept. 13. The writer Sebastian Junger and Gianna Toboni, a former Vice News correspondent, will become contributors, along with Trevor Phillips, a British journalist who joined CBS last month. Norah O’Donnell, the former anchor of “CBS Evening News,” will be a correspondent as well.

They are the first significant hires at the long-running Sunday program since CBS’s new editor in chief, Bari Weiss, orchestrated a shake-up that led to the departure of three top correspondents this spring, including the veteran journalist Scott Pelley.

Ms. Weiss has been trying to rebuild the “60 Minutes” staff in recent weeks after a tumultuous period. In moves that rattled the program’s personnel, she dismissed the correspondents Sharyn Alfonsi and Cecilia Vega, along with the show’s senior leadership team, including its former executive producer Tanya Simon.

Mr. Pelley was fired after he protested those dismissals in a clash with management; a fourth correspondent, Anderson Cooper, left voluntarily.

Correspondents on “60 Minutes” are full-time reporters who produce in-depth stories, while contributors add analysis, opinion and, periodically, reporting.

The appointment of Mr. Douthat, a conservative columnist and author, is one of the most notable hires made so far by Ms. Weiss and Nick Bilton, who succeeded Ms. Simon as executive producer in May.

Mr. Douthat joined The Times in 2009. He hosts a popular Times podcast, “Interesting Times,” where he has interviewed newsmakers including Vice President JD Vance, the “Andor” creator Tony Gilroy and former Senator Ben Sasse of Nebraska.

Katie Kingsbury, the opinion editor at The Times, said in a memo to her staff that Mr. Douthat made the case for “a religiously serious, intellectually restless conservatism.”

“He was right about things early, wrong about things honestly and never, not once, boring,” she wrote.

The stakes are high for “60 Minutes” to prove its journalistic mettle next season. The three correspondents fired from the show have said executives at CBS News tried to inject political bias into their segments. CBS News has denied those claims, and Ms. Weiss has said so-called editorial interference is part of her job as editor in chief.

Ms. Weiss asked Mr. Bilton, a tech journalist and documentarian with no experience in broadcast news, to expand “60 Minutes” beyond a one-hour weekly broadcast and integrate the program more closely into the rest of CBS’s news division. In memos to the “60 Minutes” staff, Mr. Bilton said he wanted to modernize the show without compromising the values that made it a pacesetter in TV journalism for nearly six decades.
